method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement' (published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022)), 17 claims; LICENCE: CC BY (open access; 'distributed under the terms of the CC-BY License') (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC9092201). S2: QUOTED from Commons RJ, Charles J, Cheney J, Lynar SA, et al., Diabetes Feet Australia / Australian Diabetes-related Foot Disease Guidelines panel, Journal of Foot and Ankle Research 15:47 (endorsed by nine national bodies including ASID and the Australian Diabetes Society) 'Australian guideline on management of diabetes-related foot infection: part of the 2021 Australian evidence-based guidelines for diabetes-related foot disease' (published 9 June 2022 (adapts the 2019 IWGDF infection guideline)), 10 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC9178854). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the Australian diabetes-related foot infection guideline (Diabetes Feet Australia 2021, published 2022), for diabetic foot osteomyelitis; every S1 claim is unchanged. S2's Tables 1-3 and supplementary tables were stripped and not used. The consensus statement's Tables 1–4 (diagnostic accuracy, empirical regimens, oral drug options and doses, durations) and Supplement 2 were not used: tables were stripped and the supplement was not retrieved.

claims.claim: **Do not order plain x-rays or CT routinely for suspected osteomyelitis;** they are neither sensitive nor specific enough. They still help when fracture, tumour or a foreign body is the leading concern, or when pretest probability is low (15% or less).
claims.source_text: Based on observational studies, we do not recommend the routine use of plain x-rays (because of inadequate sensitivity, specificity) or computed tomography scans (inadequate sensitivity) for all patients with a possible diagnosis of osteomyelitis (Table 1; eTable 1 in Supplement 2) as they may result in unnecessary radiation and use of resources. However, these studies may be helpful if a fracture or other noninfectious cause of bone pain (eg, tumor, foreign object) is prioritized on the differential diagnosis, and/or the pretest probability of osteomyelitis is lower (eg, ≤15%).
claims.locator: WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321, 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement', published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092201/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **MRI and certain tagged white cell scans are the most accurate imaging.** Inflammatory markers are not accurate enough to diagnose osteomyelitis.
claims.source_text: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and certain tagged white cell scans are the most accurate imaging modalities for diagnosing osteomyelitis. Inflammatory biomarkers are insufficiently accurate, and we do not recommend their routine use for osteomyelitis diagnosis.
claims.locator: WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321, 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement', published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092201/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Take blood cultures if the patient is systemically unwell or at risk of bacteraemia** (e.g. injecting drug use): a likely pathogen such as S. aureus can target therapy and may make bone biopsy unnecessary. A positive bone biopsy is highly accurate, but a negative one does not exclude infection.
claims.source_text: Blood cultures have variable sensitivity, but if the patient has systemic symptoms or risk factors for bacteremia (eg, intravenous drug use), isolating likely pathogens (eg, Staphylococcus aureus) can be helpful to target with therapy and potentially obviate the need for bone biopsy. If available, bone biopsy for histopathology is highly accurate if positive, but cannot rule out osteomyelitis if negative.
claims.locator: WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321, 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement', published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092201/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Diabetic foot:** probe-to-bone is a simple bedside test with reasonable accuracy and may avoid imaging. Use percutaneous bone biopsy for cultures where available; surface swabs are inaccurate and not recommended.
claims.source_text: The probe-to-bone (PTB) test is simple, noninvasive, and has reasonable sensitivity and specificity as a diagnostic method for DFO, which may preclude the need for imaging in some settings. … If available, percutaneous bone biopsy for deep microbiological cultures may help target antimicrobial therapy; surface cultures are not accurate and not recommended.
claims.locator: WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321, 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement', published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092201/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Osteomyelitis under a pressure ulcer:** avoid routine antibiotics unless deep bone biopsy confirms infection and surgical closure is planned, or there is sepsis or local soft-tissue infection. All patients need nutrition, debridement, off-loading and psychosocial care.
claims.source_text: Therefore, it may be preferable to avoid the routine use of antibiotic therapy for osteomyelitis underlying a pressure ulcer unless deep bone biopsy confirms osteomyelitis and surgical wound closure is planned, or the patient has accompanying sepsis syndrome or local soft tissue infection. Irrespective of antibiotic use, a multimodal therapeutic approach includes nutritional optimization, wound debridement and care, pressure off-loading, and psychosocial management.
claims.locator: WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321, 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement', published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092201/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **In a clinically stable patient without a known pathogen, it is reasonable to delay antibiotics until bone or joint samples are taken.** Do not delay when there is sepsis or threatened spinal cord compression.
claims.source_text: it is reasonable to consider deferring antimicrobial therapy initiation until bone and/or joint microbiological samples are obtained for clinically stable patients. … Decisions regarding the delay of empirical therapy therefore balance potential harm due to the risk of progression of life-threatening infection (eg, sepsis) or impending spinal cord compression against the potential benefit of microbiological data.
claims.locator: WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321, 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement', published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092201/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If antibiotics cannot wait for cultures, cover aerobic gram-positive cocci (especially S. aureus) and gram-negative bacilli,** guided by local susceptibility, patient risk factors and previous cultures, then narrow to culture results.
claims.source_text: if antibiotic therapy cannot be delayed until culture availability, it is reasonable to empirically cover aerobic gram-positive cocci, especially S aureus, and gram-negative bacilli … In all cases, local susceptibility patterns, patient-specific risk factors, and prior culture data influence the choice of antibiotic selection. Culture results can be used to tailor empirical therapy when possible.
claims.locator: WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321, 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement', published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092201/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **MRSA cover depends on local prevalence and risk:** known colonisation is the biggest single risk factor. With low local MRSA, no colonisation or prior positive cultures and little healthcare contact, it can be withheld.
claims.source_text: inclusion of empirical anti-MRSA coverage depends on local prevalence and patient-specific risk factors, such as known colonization status (which is the biggest individual risk factor), prior positive cultures, and health care exposure. In a setting with low MRSA incidence, no known MRSA colonization or prior positive cultures, and minimal health care contact, it is reasonable to withhold empirical MRSA coverage.
claims.locator: WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321, 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement', published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092201/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Antipseudomonal cover is not routine.** Add it for chronic wounds with multiple prior antibiotic courses, previous Pseudomonas, gangrene, surgery within about 3 months (e.g. early PJI), or sites linked to Pseudomonas such as malignant otitis externa.
claims.source_text: routine use of empirical antipseudomonal therapy for osteomyelitis is unnecessary. Such agents are added in the presence of specific risk factors, including patients with chronic wounds who have: (1) been exposed to multiple prior courses of antibiotics; (2) previously had cultures positive for P aeruginosa; (3) gangrenous wounds; (4) had a recent surgical procedure (eg, within 3 months, as with early PJI); or (5) specific sites of infection particularly associated with pseudomonal infection (eg, malignant otitis externa).
claims.locator: WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321, 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement', published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092201/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Adjunctive rifampicin: evidence is mixed.** Use it on culture results (mainly gram-positive cocci) weighing adverse effects and interactions (e.g. oral anticoagulants, opioids); 450–600 mg per dose is likely better than 300 mg given several times a day.
claims.source_text: Overall, the data are mixed and remain uncertain (eFigures 1 and 2 in Supplement 2). The use of rifampin in this setting is based on culture results (principally targeting gram-positive cocci or nonfermenting gram-negative bacilli) and individual patient risk-benefit considerations, acknowledging the uncertainty of the efficacy data, side effects, and potential drug interactions (especially those disrupting stable, chronic medications, such as oral anticoagulants or opiates). Studies have not elucidated optimal total daily dosing, except that 450 to 600 mg per dose likely increases pharmacodynamic target attainment and adherence compared with 300 mg multiple daily dosing.
claims.locator: WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321, 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement', published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092201/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ✅ **Oral antibiotics are a reasonable option for any type of osteomyelitis** (haematogenous, contiguous including vertebral and diabetic foot, or prosthetic), based on 8 RCTs against IV therapy, if the patient: is clinically stable; has adequate source control with no persistent bacteraemia; can absorb from a working gut; has a published oral regimen covering the likely pathogens; and has no psychosocial barrier to safe oral treatment.
claims.source_text: Based on 8 concordant RCTs comparing intravenous (IV) to oral therapy, (Figure; eFigure 3 in Supplement 2) and 9 RCTs in which oral therapy was predominantly used in both arms, we recommend oral antibiotic therapy with a drug and/or dose used in published studies as a reasonable option for osteomyelitis of any type (ie, hematogenous, prosthetic, and contiguous, the latter including vertebral and DFO) for patients who: (1) are clinically stable (hemodynamically and at the site of infection, eg, no spinal instability); (2) have adequate source control (ie, not requiring further procedural drainage and without persistent bacteremia); (3) are likely to absorb oral medications from a functioning gastrointestinal tract; (4) have an available regimen used in published osteomyelitis studies to cover likely target pathogens; and (5) have no psychosocial reasons that preclude the safe use of oral therapy.
claims.locator: WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321, 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement', published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092201/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **No minimum IV lead-in is needed:** switch to oral as soon as all the criteria are met, even during empirical therapy.
claims.source_text: There is no required minimum duration of IV lead-in; patients may be switched to oral therapy when all the above criteria are met, even at the empirical therapy stage.
claims.locator: WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321, 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement', published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092201/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ✅ **Without a retained implant, give no more than 6 weeks of antibiotics** for haematogenous or contiguous osteomyelitis (including diabetic foot), provided source control is adequate (no undrained abscess too big for antibiotics alone, possibly 2–3 cm or more).
claims.source_text: we recommend a maximum of 6 weeks of antibiotic therapy for hematogenous or contiguous pyogenic osteomyelitis (including DFO), assuming adequate source control (ie, no undrained abscesses too large to be treated with antibiotics alone, possibly ≥2-3 cm in diameter) and no retained prosthetic implant
claims.locator: WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321, 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement', published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092201/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **After debridement, 3 or 4 weeks may be enough** (small RCTs; confirmation needed). After confident total resection of infected bone, antibiotics can be omitted, or limited to 2 to 5 days if there is no soft-tissue infection.
claims.source_text: 3 or 4 weeks may be a reasonable duration of antibiotics for debrided osteomyelitis, whether hematogenous or contiguous (including DFO); however, confirmatory data are desired. Based on observational studies and 1 small RCT, it is reasonable to refrain from antibiotic use after total resection of infected bone if the treating physicians are confident that all infected bone has been resected. If administered, we do not recommend exceeding 2 to 5 days of therapy if there is no complicating soft tissue infection.
claims.locator: WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321, 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement', published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092201/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Prosthetic joint infection managed with debridement, antibiotics and implant retention (DAIR): 12 weeks is preferred over 6** (DATIPO trial). After prosthesis exchange, some experts prefer 12 weeks, while others see equipoise, especially when the pathogen is not S. aureus.
claims.source_text: participating experts unanimously agree that 12 is preferred to 6 weeks of antibiotics for PJI treated with debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention (DAIR). Some experts also clearly preferred 12 weeks of antibiotics for PJI treated with prosthetic exchanges. However, others believed that equipoise remains between 6 vs 12 weeks for these patients, particularly if S aureus is not the etiologic pathogen, or for 1-stage exchanges or 2-stage revisions with negative cultures prior to implantation.
claims.locator: WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321, 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement', published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092201/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Other infected implants (e.g. fracture fixation):** one approach is to treat until the bone has healed enough for the hardware to come out. Chronic oral suppression is an option when curative surgery is too risky, though its risks and benefits are poorly defined.
claims.source_text: A reasonable strategy, without evidence for or against, may be to treat with antibiotics until the bone heals sufficiently enough that the implants can be removed, such as in cases of fracture. Finally, chronic oral suppressive therapy may be considered for patients for whom the risks and benefits of curative surgery is deemed unacceptable; however, available data have not defined the risks and benefits of this approach well to this point.
claims.locator: WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321, 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement', published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092201/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Initial tests for suspected diabetic foot osteomyelitis: combine the probe-to-bone test, ESR (or CRP and/or procalcitonin) and plain x-rays** (strong; moderate). If the x-ray, clinical and laboratory findings are most compatible with osteomyelitis, no further foot imaging is needed to make the diagnosis (strong; low).
claims.source_text: In a person with diabetes and suspected osteomyelitis of the foot, we recommend using a combination of the probe-to-bone test, the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (or C-reactive protein and/or procalcitonin), and plain X-rays as the initial studies to diagnose osteomyelitis. (Strong; moderate). … if a plain X-ray and clinical and laboratory findings are most compatible with osteomyelitis, we recommend no further imaging of the foot to establish the diagnosis. (Strong; low).
claims.locator: Commons RJ, Charles J, Cheney J, Lynar SA, et al., Diabetes Feet Australia / Australian Diabetes-related Foot Disease Guidelines panel, Journal of Foot and Ankle Research 15:47 (endorsed by nine national bodies including ASID and the Australian Diabetes Society), 'Australian guideline on management of diabetes-related foot infection: part of the 2021 Australian evidence-based guidelines for diabetes-related foot disease', published 9 June 2022 (adapts the 2019 IWGDF infection guideline), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9178854/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **If the diagnosis remains in doubt, consider MRI, 18F-FDG-PET/CT or leukocyte scintigraphy (with or without CT)** (strong; moderate).
claims.source_text: If the diagnosis of osteomyelitis remains in doubt, consider ordering an advanced imaging study, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan, 18F-FDG-positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) or leukocyte scintigraphy (with or without CT). (Strong; moderate).
claims.locator: Commons RJ, Charles J, Cheney J, Lynar SA, et al., Diabetes Feet Australia / Australian Diabetes-related Foot Disease Guidelines panel, Journal of Foot and Ankle Research 15:47 (endorsed by nine national bodies including ASID and the Australian Diabetes Society), 'Australian guideline on management of diabetes-related foot infection: part of the 2021 Australian evidence-based guidelines for diabetes-related foot disease', published 9 June 2022 (adapts the 2019 IWGDF infection guideline), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9178854/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Take a bone sample (percutaneous or surgical) for culture and, if possible, histopathology when a definitive diagnosis or the causative pathogen is needed to choose treatment** (strong; low). The panel notes that expertise in percutaneous bone biopsy is low in many Australian locations.
claims.source_text: in whom making a definitive diagnosis or determining the causative pathogen is necessary for selecting treatment, collect a sample of bone (percutaneously or surgically) to culture clinically relevant bone microorganisms and for histopathology (if possible). (Strong; low). … although expertise for percutaneous biopsy was noted to be low in many Australian locations.
claims.locator: Commons RJ, Charles J, Cheney J, Lynar SA, et al., Diabetes Feet Australia / Australian Diabetes-related Foot Disease Guidelines panel, Journal of Foot and Ankle Research 15:47 (endorsed by nine national bodies including ASID and the Australian Diabetes Society), 'Australian guideline on management of diabetes-related foot infection: part of the 2021 Australian evidence-based guidelines for diabetes-related foot disease', published 9 June 2022 (adapts the 2019 IWGDF infection guideline), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9178854/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Uncomplicated forefoot osteomyelitis with no other reason for surgery: consider antibiotics without surgical bone resection** (strong; moderate). 'Uncomplicated' means no severe (grade 4) infection, necrotising tissue infection, bone exposed in the base of the ulcer, kidney injury or peripheral artery disease.
claims.source_text: In a patient with diabetes and uncomplicated forefoot osteomyelitis, for whom there is no other indication for surgical treatment, consider treating with antibiotic therapy without surgical resection of bone. (Strong; moderate). … uncomplicated forefoot osteomyelitis should be defined as osteomyelitis without severe (grade 4) infection, and without any of the following: necrotising tissue infection, bone exposed in the base of the ulcer, kidney injury, or peripheral artery disease.
claims.locator: Commons RJ, Charles J, Cheney J, Lynar SA, et al., Diabetes Feet Australia / Australian Diabetes-related Foot Disease Guidelines panel, Journal of Foot and Ankle Research 15:47 (endorsed by nine national bodies including ASID and the Australian Diabetes Society), 'Australian guideline on management of diabetes-related foot infection: part of the 2021 Australian evidence-based guidelines for diabetes-related foot disease', published 9 June 2022 (adapts the 2019 IWGDF infection guideline), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9178854/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Probable diabetic foot osteomyelitis with soft-tissue infection: urgently evaluate the need for surgery,** with intensive post-operative medical and surgical follow-up (strong; moderate).
claims.source_text: In a patient with probable diabetes-related foot osteomyelitis with concomitant soft tissue infection, urgently evaluate the need for surgery as well as intensive post-operative medical and surgical follow-up. (Strong; moderate).
claims.locator: Commons RJ, Charles J, Cheney J, Lynar SA, et al., Diabetes Feet Australia / Australian Diabetes-related Foot Disease Guidelines panel, Journal of Foot and Ankle Research 15:47 (endorsed by nine national bodies including ASID and the Australian Diabetes Society), 'Australian guideline on management of diabetes-related foot infection: part of the 2021 Australian evidence-based guidelines for diabetes-related foot disease', published 9 June 2022 (adapts the 2019 IWGDF infection guideline), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9178854/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Choose antibiotics with demonstrated efficacy for osteomyelitis** (strong; low); the drugs used for non-diabetic osteomyelitis are reasonable, including beta-lactams, beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitors, (fluoro)quinolones, glycopeptides and lipoglycopeptides, oxazolidinones, sulfonamides, lincosamides, rifamycins and fusidic acid.
claims.source_text: Select antibiotic agents for treating diabetes-related foot osteomyelitis from among those that have demonstrated efficacy for osteomyelitis in clinical studies. (Strong; low). … it would be reasonable to use antibiotics that are used for osteomyelitis that is not associated with diabetes-related foot infections. Such antibiotics include beta-lactams, beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitors, (fluoro) quinolones, glycopeptides and lipoglycopeptides, oxazolidinones, sulfonamides, lincosamides, rifamycins and fusidic acid
claims.locator: Commons RJ, Charles J, Cheney J, Lynar SA, et al., Diabetes Feet Australia / Australian Diabetes-related Foot Disease Guidelines panel, Journal of Foot and Ankle Research 15:47 (endorsed by nine national bodies including ASID and the Australian Diabetes Society), 'Australian guideline on management of diabetes-related foot infection: part of the 2021 Australian evidence-based guidelines for diabetes-related foot disease', published 9 June 2022 (adapts the 2019 IWGDF infection guideline), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9178854/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **If parenteral therapy was needed at first, consider switching to a highly bioavailable oral antibiotic after perhaps 5 to 7 days,** when the pathogens are susceptible to an available oral drug and nothing precludes oral therapy (weak; moderate).
claims.source_text: For people with diabetes-related foot osteomyelitis that initially require parenteral therapy, consider switching to an oral antibiotic regimen that has high bioavailability after perhaps 5 to 7 days, if the likely or proven pathogens are susceptible to an available oral agent and the patient has no clinical condition precluding oral therapy. (Weak; moderate).
claims.locator: Commons RJ, Charles J, Cheney J, Lynar SA, et al., Diabetes Feet Australia / Australian Diabetes-related Foot Disease Guidelines panel, Journal of Foot and Ankle Research 15:47 (endorsed by nine national bodies including ASID and the Australian Diabetes Society), 'Australian guideline on management of diabetes-related foot infection: part of the 2021 Australian evidence-based guidelines for diabetes-related foot disease', published 9 June 2022 (adapts the 2019 IWGDF infection guideline), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9178854/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Duration: the Australian panel did NOT adopt the international 'no longer than 6 weeks' recommendation for diabetic foot osteomyelitis,** judging the population too heterogeneous for it to be broadly applied. Its advice to reconsider bone culture, resection or a different regimen if there is no clinical improvement within 2 to 4 weeks was kept as a general principle.
claims.source_text: Treat diabetes-related foot osteomyelitis with antibiotic therapy for no longer than 6 weeks. If the infection does not clinically improve within the first 2 to 4 weeks, reconsider the need for collecting a bone specimen for culture, undertaking surgical resection, or selecting an alternative antibiotic regimen. (Strong; moderate). Decision: Excluded. … The population addressed (person with diabetes and osteomyelitis of the foot) was considered to be too heterogeneous for the recommendation to treat with antibiotic therapy for no longer than 6 weeks to be broadly applied. The highly select subgroup for which there is some evidence to support a shorter duration of therapy is targeted in Recommendation 21(a). The second sentence of the recommendation was considered to reflect expert opinion of good practice supported by extensive experience and considered to be a general principle rather than remain as an evidence-based recommendation.
claims.locator: Commons RJ, Charles J, Cheney J, Lynar SA, et al., Diabetes Feet Australia / Australian Diabetes-related Foot Disease Guidelines panel, Journal of Foot and Ankle Research 15:47 (endorsed by nine national bodies including ASID and the Australian Diabetes Society), 'Australian guideline on management of diabetes-related foot infection: part of the 2021 Australian evidence-based guidelines for diabetes-related foot disease', published 9 June 2022 (adapts the 2019 IWGDF infection guideline), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9178854/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **After all infected bone has been surgically removed and there is no soft-tissue infection, give antibiotics for just a few days** (weak; low), defined by the panel as 2 to 5 days, which allows time for the histopathology and culture of the residual bone margin.
claims.source_text: Treat diabetes-related foot osteomyelitis with antibiotic therapy for just a few days if there is no soft tissue infection and all the infected bone has been surgically removed. (Weak; low). … the panel believe that the duration that antibiotic therapy should be continued, described as 'just a few days' in the recommendation should be defined as 2 to 5 days. This is consistent with Australian infection guidelines and allows clinicians to await histopathology and culture results from tissue samples taken from the presumed uninfected residual bone margin to verify adequate surgical removal of infection.
claims.locator: Commons RJ, Charles J, Cheney J, Lynar SA, et al., Diabetes Feet Australia / Australian Diabetes-related Foot Disease Guidelines panel, Journal of Foot and Ankle Research 15:47 (endorsed by nine national bodies including ASID and the Australian Diabetes Society), 'Australian guideline on management of diabetes-related foot infection: part of the 2021 Australian evidence-based guidelines for diabetes-related foot disease', published 9 June 2022 (adapts the 2019 IWGDF infection guideline), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9178854/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **At resection, consider sending bone from the stump for culture (and histopathology)** (weak; moderate). If that aseptic specimen grows pathogens or the histology shows osteomyelitis, give appropriate antibiotics for up to 6 weeks (strong; moderate). From remote sites, results take longer, so continue antibiotics until they are available.
claims.source_text: During surgery to resect bone for diabetes-related foot osteomyelitis, consider obtaining a specimen of bone for culture (and, if possible, histopathology) at the stump of the resected bone to identify if there is residual bone infection. (Weak; moderate). … If an aseptically collected culture specimen obtained during the surgery grows pathogen(s), or if the histology demonstrates osteomyelitis, administer appropriate antibiotic therapy for up to 6 weeks. (Strong; moderate). … The panel noted that there may be longer turn-around times for laboratory results from bone sampling (microbiology and anatomical pathology) when sent from remote sites and that this should be considered in the treatment algorithm. Antibiotics should be continued until the results are available.
claims.locator: Commons RJ, Charles J, Cheney J, Lynar SA, et al., Diabetes Feet Australia / Australian Diabetes-related Foot Disease Guidelines panel, Journal of Foot and Ankle Research 15:47 (endorsed by nine national bodies including ASID and the Australian Diabetes Society), 'Australian guideline on management of diabetes-related foot infection: part of the 2021 Australian evidence-based guidelines for diabetes-related foot disease', published 9 June 2022 (adapts the 2019 IWGDF infection guideline), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9178854/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Do not follow ESR, CRP or repeat imaging routinely;** neither predicts long-term cure for the individual patient. Repeat imaging when a patient is failing therapy, to guide source control, find complications such as pathological fracture, or rethink the diagnosis.
claims.source_text: observational studies have generally found that neither serial inflammatory biomarkers (eg, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein) nor routinely repeated imaging accurately predict long-term treatment success for osteomyelitis or PJI for individual patients, nor have they been shown to meaningfully alter treatment decisions beyond clinical observation. Thus, following inflammatory biomarkers and repeated imaging may not offer benefit or contribute to high value care in most patients. Nonetheless, repeated imaging may be useful for patients who are clinically failing therapy to inform source control attempts, identify mechanical complications such as pathological fracture, and/or to trigger reconsideration of the initial diagnosis.
claims.locator: WikiGuidelines Group (Spellberg B et al.), JAMA Network Open 5(5):e2211321, 'Use of Novel Strategies to Develop Guidelines for Management of Pyogenic Osteomyelitis in Adults: A WikiGuidelines Group Consensus Statement', published 11 May 2022 (evidence to 1 March 2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092201/, retrieved 2026-09-23
